query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle failure does not primarily stem from classical grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation as in conventional alloys, but from a threshold-dependent dynamic amorphization of high-angle grain boundaries that induces localized cavitation under high-strain or low-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a homogeneous microstructure and minimal pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates or segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high-strain rate deformation tests at low temperatures to stress the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: High mechanical strain rates and subambient service temperatures where conventional ductile mechanisms are suppressed, creating conditions that favor stress-induced amorphization at the grain boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: High-angle grain boundaries in the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Applied stress activates a dynamic amorphization mechanism at the high-angle grain boundaries, leading to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer that eventually undergoes cavitation. This structural transition undermines the alloy’s capacity to deform plastically, promoting brittle failure, which contrasts with the segregation/precipitation-driven embrittlement typical of conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial ductile baseline, the high-entropy alloy will show a pronounced drop in toughness upon reaching a critical strain or temperature threshold. Microstructural analysis will reveal localized amorphization and nanoporosity at high-angle grain boundaries, which would not be observed in conventional alloys under the same test conditions.
generation.baseline: The alloy initially exhibits a uniform single-phase microstructure with well-bonded, stable grain boundaries, showing ductile behavior under moderate strain rates and temperatures.
generation.boundary: This brittle failure mechanism is expected to be activated only under high-strain (or high-strain-rate) and/or low-temperature conditions, while under typical service conditions the alloy maintains its favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact strain rate and temperature thresholds for initiating dynamic amorphization and cavitation are not predetermined and require further experimental calibration. The magnitude of toughness loss also remains to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled comparative deformation study between the high-entropy alloy and a conventional alloy with analogous grain size. Both alloys are subjected to high-strain rate tests at low temperatures while monitoring changes in fracture toughness and microstructural evolution. Electron microscopy (e.g., STEM) should be used pre- and post-deformation to assess the presence of amorphous layers and cavitation at the grain boundaries.
measurements: Extent of nanoporosity/cavitation featuring in the deformed state
Threshold strain and temperature for transition from ductile to brittle behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a distinct threshold-induced loss in toughness accompanied by grain-boundary amorphization and cavitation under high-strain/low-temperature conditions (or if such features appear equally in the conventional alloy), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
